claims.text: Reducing local atomic disorder in high-entropy superconductors increases superconducting critical temperature.
Reducing local atomic disorder enhances electron–phonon coupling.
The initial materials are single-phase, compositionally disordered high-entropy alloy superconductors in the dirty limit.
Controlled annealing is proposed to reduce short-range disorder without changing bulk composition.
Replacing an element with a chemically similar species having comparable valence electron count and lower atomic-size variance is proposed to reduce disorder.
Samples with identical bulk composition but different local atomic order provide a controlled comparison of disorder effects.
Short-range atomic order or local chemical homogeneity is the structural mediator linking processing to superconducting behavior.
Short-range atomic order can be assessed using X-ray diffraction or local electron microscopy.
Reduced local disorder stabilizes vibrational modes.
Reduced local disorder minimizes electron scattering.
Enhanced electron–phonon coupling supports stronger Cooper pairing and a higher critical temperature.
Reduced-disorder samples will have a higher critical temperature than as-cast, more-disordered samples.
Reduced-disorder samples will have a sharper superconducting transition than the baseline.
A sharper superconducting transition would reflect enhanced electron–phonon interaction.
Electron count and degree of disorder can affect superconductivity in this alloy family.
The predicted disorder effect applies only when valence electron count and macroscopic phase purity are maintained.
The proposed relationship may cease to be predictable at extremely low disorder approaching crystalline order.
Failure of successfully ordered samples to show a statistically significant increase in critical temperature and a sharper transition would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: Element substitution is offered as an intervention while the comparison is also required to retain identical bulk or overall elemental composition. Replacing one element necessarily changes elemental identity, so that branch is not composition-matched to the stated baseline.

The intervention permits elemental substitution, but the boundary excludes significant composition changes and requires valence electron count to remain fixed; no substitution is specified that demonstrably satisfies both constraints.
